Modern CPUs execute what is called microcode. When you compile an application (.exe on windows) it is compiled into machine language (Intel 386 w/AMD64 + the various zillion extensions and features like SSE). The machine language instructions on Intel and AMD CPUs are then internally re-interpreted on the CPU and executed by the microcode running on the CPU. A single machine code instruction may represent dozens of microcode instructions. The why of this is a deep answer and I'll completely ignore it. If you care you can explore the history of CISC and RISC instruction sets and how they became something else internally to CPUs.

When your computer first boots it loads the current microcode into the CPU. This allows many classes of hardware bugs to be worked around by changing how instructions are internally executed. Recently a long list of hardware bugs have been exposed which allow intelligence agencies and other nefarious applications (spyware, trojans, viruses) to directly read protected information from memory which would otherwise be prohibited by the operating system (windows/linux/ios). Since these are hardware bugs there is usually little the OS can do to maintain protection. Which means everyone running these buggy CPUs are vulnerable. When the CPU/microcode can do something it usually carries significant performance impact. In this case, it absolutely does. The impact ranges from 2% - 60+%, depending on the nature of the workload.

The current microcode fixes some of the remaining security issues. These security issues are very serious. The fixed also impose significant performance loss for many workloads. Sure, we had Wine, and Lutris, but many PC Gamers are not tech savvy, despite what they might think, and balk at doing anything truly technical on their PCs. Valve's Steam Play offers them an alternative.

How do I Opt into Steam Play?

Steam Play is currently in beta, so in order to use it, you would first need to opt into the Steam Beta Client release.

To do this, Launch Steam, then go to Steam > Settings, and then on the Account page, locate the Beta Participation section and click on Change.

From the drop down list, select Steam Beta Update and click OK. You'll be asked to restart Steam.

Once the Beta Client of Steam has been installed, return to Steam > Settings and you should now see a new section at the bottom marked Steam Play.

I Can't Install X Game, Why?

The game is probably not on the official whitelist yet, which means Valve have not tested and confirmed the game will work to the standards which are required for a game to be Steam Play ready.

You can turn on Steam Play for all games, if you wish, but remember, not every game will work.

To turn on Steam Play for every game, return to Steam > Settings, and click on the Steam Play section.

Tick the two boxes "Enable Steam Play for All Titles" and "Use this Tool Instead of Game-Specific Selections from Steam".

Restart the Steam Client.

If Proton is just Modified Wine, where are the Wineprefixes Stored?

Steam will store Wineprefixes in the following location:

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/compatdata

Within that folder you will see subfolders named as a bunch of numbers. These are the Steam AppIDs for each game you are trying to run using Steam Play. Within each of these folders you will find a "pfx" folder, and this is where the Wineprefix for that game begins.

I checked and there aren't any game files in those pfx folders, where did Steam store the game files?

All game files are stored in the default Steam location, within their own folders.

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/common

A game I want to run requires X windows component or DLL override to work, can I still set these manually?

Winetricks should work if you target the pfx folder with the WINEPREFIX= environment variable, though your mileage will vary, depending on what you are attempting to install into the pfx folder.

I need to set a game to not use DXVK, or default to the DX9 version, how can I do that?

By settings launch options for each game in Steam, you can change how Proton will attempt to launch the game. The following environment variables are accepted as launch options:

Compat config string Environment Variable Description
wined3d11 PROTON_USE_WINED3D11 Use OpenGL-based wined3d instead of Vulkan-based DXVK for d3d11.
nod3d11 PROTON_NO_D3D11 Disable d3d11.dll, for games which can fall back to and run better with d3d9.
noesync PROTON_NO_ESYNC Do not use eventfd-based in-process synchronization primitives.

So, in order to set a game to not use ESync, you would set the launch options to:

PROTON_NO_ESYNC=1 %command%

What if I want to apply Global Settings?

Global Settings can be applied by renaming the file "user_settings.sample.py" to "user_settings.py" and then editting the config file to remove the "#" symbol from whatever setting you want applied to every game you launch via Steam Play.

The config file can be found under:

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/common/Proton {Version_Number}/
